paragraphs: Watermarking makes machine-generated text identifiable by embedding a hidden signal during generation. The difficulty is adding that signal while preserving the language model’s original distribution of outputs. This paper introduces DiPmark, which combines distribution preservation with detection that does not require access to the model’s API or the prompts used to generate the text.

Before generating a word, DiPmark randomly selects a set of tokens. It then uses a distribution-preserving reweighting function that increases the selected tokens’ sampling probabilities. The important distinction is between this local preference and the distribution-preserving property of the overall watermarking procedure: the method is designed to introduce a detectable signal while retaining the original token distribution.

The paper also provides a robustness guarantee for moderate token changes, giving its resilience claim a specific scope. Evaluations across language models and tasks support the stated combination of distribution preservation, accessible detection, and resistance to edits. Together, these properties address both generation quality and the practical problem of recognizing watermarked text after it has been modified.
icml-2024-a-resilient-and-accessible-dis.tldr: DiPmark embeds detectable text watermarks while preserving token distributions and providing robustness to moderate token changes.

paragraphs: This paper develops a learning-theory framework for choosing models that tolerate faults. Its fault-tolerant PAC formulation asks how much training data is needed to identify the most fault-tolerant models within a specified hypothesis class, such as a collection of neural networks. It makes faults part of the learning problem itself.

The results distinguish random faults from adversarial ones. When faults occur randomly, fault-tolerant learning is equivalent to ordinary PAC learning. With adversarial faults, however, the required number of examples can grow linearly with the number of fault-induced perturbing functions. This difficulty can arise even for a hypothesis class with VC dimension one, showing that a simple model class alone does not remove the learning burden.

The authors establish a matching upper bound when the number of perturbing functions is restricted. They also show that neural-network deletion faults permit substantially better dependence on that number. The findings therefore connect learning difficulty to both the number and the structure of possible faults, rather than treating fault tolerance as a single uniform requirement.
icml-2024-a-theory-of-fault-tolerant-lea.tldr: A theoretical framework shows how the type and variety of faults determine the data needed to learn fault-tolerant models.

paragraphs: AND explains acoustic networks at the level of individual neurons. It examines audio that strongly activates a neuron and automatically produces a natural-language description of what those recordings share. Large language models summarize common acoustic features and identities, turning activation patterns into descriptions that people can inspect.

Experiments support the precision and informativeness of these descriptions. The resulting analysis suggests that the studied models distinguish audio through combinations of basic acoustic features rather than primarily through abstract concepts. It also reveals differences associated with training strategy: supervised training progressively narrows neurons’ attention, while self-supervised training encourages neurons to respond to multiple meanings or patterns as they explore higher-level features.

These findings make the framework useful for studying how acoustic representations develop, beyond simply naming what a neuron responds to. The paper also demonstrates a potential application to model unlearning: descriptions guide the pruning of neurons associated with particular concepts. That demonstration presents concept-specific pruning as a possible use of the interpretation framework, rather than establishing a general solution to unlearning.
icml-2024-and-audio-network-dissection-f.tldr: AND describes acoustic neurons in natural language and uses those descriptions to analyze training effects and explore concept-specific pruning.

paragraphs: Reinforcement learning becomes harder when an event happens well before an agent receives the corresponding sensory information. Existing methods that expand the state representation to handle these delays can create an enormous state space or lose performance when the environment is stochastic. This paper addresses the learning difficulty created by long feedback delays.

Auxiliary-Delayed Reinforcement Learning, or AD-RL, uses tasks with shorter delays to help solve the longer-delay problem. It first learns a value function in the short-delay setting. Bootstrapping and policy improvement then adapt that value information to the long-delay setting. The central idea is to use an easier timing regime as a source of guidance for the harder one.

The theoretical analysis shows that this approach can substantially reduce sample complexity, meaning the amount of experience required for learning. Experiments on both deterministic and stochastic benchmarks report improvements over state-of-the-art methods in sample efficiency and policy performance. These results support auxiliary short delays as a useful training mechanism that also works in the tested environments with randomness.
icml-2024-boosting-reinforcement-learnin.tldr: AD-RL transfers value information from short-delay tasks to improve learning efficiency and policy performance under long feedback delays.

paragraphs: Dueling bandits learn from preferences between pairs of items, as can arise in ranking or recommendation. This paper studies how to find the item with the highest Borda score while limiting cumulative regret, the accumulated cost of choices that fall short of the objective. Its generalized linear model family includes many existing dueling-bandit models.

The authors prove that Borda regret has a lower bound of order d^(2/3) T^(2/3), where d is the context-vector dimension and T is the number of rounds. For the stochastic setting, they develop an explore-then-commit algorithm whose upper bound nearly matches this rate, up to logarithmic factors. This links the algorithm’s performance to a fundamental difficulty of the problem.

They also develop an EXP3-type algorithm for an adversarial linear setting, in which the underlying parameter can change every round. It achieves the same stated regret order up to logarithmic factors and is described as optimal. Experiments using synthetic data and a simulated real-world environment corroborate the theoretical analysis across the investigated settings.
icml-2024-borda-regret-minimization-for-.tldr: The paper establishes near-matching regret bounds and algorithms for learning Borda-optimal choices from pairwise preferences.

paragraphs: Selective classification allows a model to decline predictions when its confidence is insufficient. Its goal is to improve reliability among the predictions it does make. While earlier approaches mainly modify the final classification layers to estimate confidence, this paper investigates how the learned feature representation can improve the decision to predict or abstain.

A generalization bound motivates optimizing the feature layers. The proposed method, Confidence-aware Contrastive Learning for Selective Classification, brings features of homogeneous instances closer together and pushes heterogeneous instances apart. The model’s confidence controls the strength of these adjustments. Confidence therefore influences how the representation is learned, rather than serving only as a threshold applied after classification.

On CIFAR-10, CIFAR-100, CelebA, and ImageNet, the method achieves lower selective risk than state-of-the-art alternatives across almost all tested coverage levels. Coverage describes how often the model chooses to predict, so the result concerns reliability across different amounts of abstention. The method can also be combined with existing approaches to improve performance further.
icml-2024-confidence-aware-contrastive-l.tldr: Confidence-aware feature learning improves the accuracy of predictions retained by selective classifiers across almost all tested coverage levels.

paragraphs: Medical visual question answering must connect a user’s instruction to relevant evidence in a medical image. Diverse imagery and inadequate annotations make this difficult. Uni-Med addresses the connection between instructions, visual evidence, and answers, with the aim of making the basis for a response easier to trace.

Its Instruct-to-Answer Clues Interpreter generates visual explanations using answers and labels the central part of each instruction as its real intent. This process produces the publicly available IAI-Med VQA dataset. A Token-Level Cut-Mix module dynamically aligns explanations with image patches, while intention-guided attention reduces interference from instruction content outside the core request. Together, these components give training more explicit guidance about what the question asks and where its evidence lies.

Experiments on SLAKE report 87.52% accuracy for closed questions and 86.12% overall accuracy. The abstract reports respective improvements of 1.22% and 0.92% over MedVInT-PMC-VQA. These results support the framework’s effectiveness on the evaluated question-answering tasks, alongside its contribution of explanation and intent annotations.
icml-2024-detecting-any-instruction-to-a.tldr: Uni-Med connects instruction intent with image evidence to improve medical visual question answering and make answers more traceable.

paragraphs: Individual treatment effect estimation aims to predict how a treatment affects a particular sample or person. The paper addresses a tension between predictive accuracy and faithful explanations. Black-box models may predict well without explaining themselves, while explanations added afterward lack faithfulness guarantees and existing self-interpretable approaches can sacrifice substantial accuracy.

DISCRET builds rule-based explanations into the estimation framework. Its key idea is to use an explanation as a database query that identifies a subgroup of similar samples. This connects the explanation to the framework’s operation: the rules do useful work in selecting relevant samples rather than merely describing a completed prediction. A reinforcement-learning algorithm searches the large space of possible explanations efficiently.

Evaluations cover tasks involving tabular data, images, and text. DISCRET outperforms the strongest self-interpretable models considered and achieves accuracy comparable to the strongest black-box models while supplying faithful explanations. The findings support using sample-specific rules as part of treatment-effect estimation without the large accuracy compromise attributed to earlier interpretable methods.
icml-2024-discret-synthesizing-faithful-.tldr: DISCRET uses rule-based subgroup queries to provide faithful treatment-effect explanations with accuracy comparable to leading black-box models.

paragraphs: A vision-language model can recognize objects in an image yet describe relationships between them incorrectly. This paper focuses on that form of hallucination, which object-focused evaluations overlook. Understanding whether objects have a particular relationship is a separate requirement for visual comprehension, beyond deciding whether those objects are present.

The authors introduce R-Bench to evaluate relationship hallucinations at two levels. Image-level questions ask whether a relationship exists, while instance-level questions test understanding of specific local visual content. Their analysis identifies three kinds of co-occurrence that lead to hallucinations: associations between relationships, between subjects and relationships, and between relationships and objects.

The paper also finds that the long-tail distribution of visual instruction-tuning data significantly affects relationship understanding. Current models tend to neglect image evidence and rely too heavily on language-model commonsense knowledge, and they struggle to reason about spatial relationships using context. These findings help explain how plausible answers can remain visually incorrect and establish a benchmark for examining that gap.
icml-2024-evaluating-and-analyzing-relat.tldr: R-Bench evaluates invented visual relationships and reveals how learned associations can outweigh image evidence in vision-language models.

paragraphs: When measurements arrive more slowly than the causal processes operating in a system, many intermediate states go unobserved. Conventional time-series causal discovery methods can then make substantial errors. One response is to compare interventions, but interventions may be costly, unethical, or infeasible in settings such as health and social science.

This paper investigates how data from only two time slices can replace intervention data to improve causal ordering. It proposes DHT-CIT, a Descendant Hierarchical Topology algorithm using conditional independence tests. The central technical ingredient is a criterion applied repeatedly to each node to identify its descendants, meaning the nodes downstream of it in the causal structure.

By organizing discovery around descendant relationships, the method extracts causal information despite the missing intermediate measurements. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report superior performance for DHT-CIT. The contribution is therefore a specific algorithm for learning from coarsely sampled observations, supported by a conditional-independence criterion and empirical results, with two time slices providing the observations used by the method.
icml-2024-learning-causal-relations-from.tldr: DHT-CIT uses conditional independence tests on two time slices to learn causal relationships from coarsely sampled time series.

paragraphs: Graph data contains dependencies between examples, and those dependencies can change between training and deployment. This makes generalization difficult because a model may learn patterns of interaction that are specific to its training distribution. The paper addresses this problem through a geometric diffusion model with learnable divergence fields.

The model generalizes the diffusion equation by making diffusivity stochastic at each time step. This is intended to capture multiple kinds of information flow among dependent data points. A learning objective derived through causal inference then guides the model toward interdependence patterns that remain insensitive to domain changes. The approach therefore addresses both how information moves and which movement patterns should be learned.

The authors implement three versions that generalize graph convolutional networks, graph attention networks, and Transformers. Evaluations on diverse real-world datasets demonstrate promising out-of-distribution performance and robustness to distribution shifts. The findings support this diffusion-based formulation as a way to improve several model families when the relationships among data points change across domains.
icml-2024-learning-divergence-fields-for.tldr: A learnable diffusion framework helps graph models capture interdependence patterns that generalize across distribution shifts.

paragraphs: Predicting how amino acid mutations change protein binding is difficult when annotated mutation data is scarce. Pretraining on unlabeled data offers a route forward, but the paper identifies challenges in representing dependencies across structural scales, capturing local conformational changes, and controlling the data and computation costs of pretraining.

The proposed framework builds a hierarchical prompt codebook that separately records common microenvironment patterns at different structural scales. A masked microenvironment modeling task trains this codebook to represent the joint relationships among mutations, residue types, angular statistics, and local conformational changes. This gives the learned patterns information about both molecular composition and the surrounding structure.

For each mutation, the framework encodes the local environment into several hierarchical prompts and combines them to inform representations of the original and mutated protein complexes. The prompts communicate differences between their microenvironments. Experiments report better mutation-effect prediction and training efficiency than state-of-the-art pretraining-based methods, including a case study on optimizing human antibodies against SARS-CoV-2.
icml-2024-learning-to-predict-mutational.tldr: Hierarchical microenvironment prompts improve prediction of mutation effects on protein binding while making training more efficient.

paragraphs: This paper asks how to change the rewards of a zero-sum Markov game so that players settle on a desired policy profile. The objective is demanding: the target must become the unique Markov perfect Nash equilibrium, its value must lie within a specified range, and the reward changes should cost as little as possible.

The setting allows either deterministic or stochastic target policies and can represent the actions of a benevolent designer or a malicious adversary. A central contribution is characterizing which policy profiles can actually be installed as the unique equilibrium. The paper supplies both necessary and sufficient conditions, making feasibility an explicit part of the problem rather than assuming every requested modification can succeed.

For constructing a modification, the authors propose an efficient algorithm that solves a convex optimization problem with linear constraints and then applies a random perturbation. The resulting modification plan has near-optimal cost. This combines a characterization of attainable outcomes with a procedure for approaching the cheapest reward change that achieves the specified equilibrium and value requirements.
icml-2024-minimally-modifying-a-markov-g.tldr: The paper characterizes feasible equilibrium-changing reward modifications and constructs near-minimum-cost plans for zero-sum Markov games.

paragraphs: Continual learning asks a model to acquire new tasks while retaining knowledge of earlier ones. Replay methods help by keeping examples from past tasks in a memory buffer. This paper argues that replay alone can underuse that history because existing approaches generally overlook relationships among the previously learned tasks.

The authors first express replay-based methods through a unified hierarchical gradient aggregation framework. This provides a common way to describe how learning signals from current and previous tasks are combined. They then introduce Pareto optimization to account for relationships among earlier tasks, producing the Pareto-Optimized Continual Learning algorithm, or POCL. Its objective is to improve overall past-task performance while maintaining performance on the current task.

The approach makes the integration of old knowledge an explicit optimization problem, rather than treating the buffer only as a collection of examples to revisit. Experiments across multiple datasets and settings show POCL outperforming the state-of-the-art continual-learning methods considered. These results support modeling interactions among previous tasks as a useful way to reduce forgetting.
icml-2024-mitigating-catastrophic-forget.tldr: POCL uses Pareto optimization to combine learning signals from past tasks and reduce forgetting while maintaining current-task performance.

paragraphs: Incorrect training labels can substantially weaken graph neural networks. Selecting useful training samples is one way to improve robustness, but methods developed for independent examples do not directly address graph dependencies. In particular, nodes near topological class boundaries can be highly informative even though heuristic selection methods struggle to distinguish them successfully.

Topological Sample Selection, or TSS, incorporates the graph’s structure into the sample-selection process. The motivation is that deciding which labeled nodes to learn from should account for their position in the graph. This addresses both the difficulty of handling informative boundary nodes and the lack of a selection measure that uses topological information.

The authors prove that their procedure minimizes an upper bound on expected risk under the target clean distribution. This is a guarantee about a bound on clean-distribution error, rather than a claim that the error itself is always minimized. Experiments also show improvements over state-of-the-art baselines, supporting graph-aware selection as a way to learn more effectively from noisy labels.
icml-2024-mitigating-label-noise-on-grap.tldr: TSS uses graph topology to select informative training samples under label noise, with theoretical and empirical support.

paragraphs: Passive observations, including video, can contain useful information for reinforcement learning even when they do not record actions. This paper investigates when such data benefits an agent that subsequently learns through interaction. Its theoretical result is conditional: passive learning is statistically beneficial when the dynamics are identifiable, so action effects can be distinguished from randomness.

The proposed Multiscale State-Centric Planners algorithm uses two planners with different scopes. A fast planner handles immediate objectives, while a slow planner guides progress toward longer-term goals. The fast planner also includes pessimistic regularization to address differences between the offline data distribution and the data encountered during online learning.

This combination is designed to handle imperfect pretraining and limited coverage in the passive dataset. Experiments across multiple benchmarks show significant improvements over existing approaches, especially in the complex, long-horizon setting emphasized by the paper. The findings pair a condition explaining when passive data helps with an algorithm that organizes that information into guidance at two planning scales.
icml-2024-planning-fast-and-slow-online-.tldr: MSCP combines immediate and long-term planners to use action-free offline observations for more effective online reinforcement learning.

paragraphs: Multi-instance point-cloud registration estimates several rigid transformations between two sets of three-dimensional points. Overlapping instances make this difficult because point correspondences can be ambiguous. Existing approaches also rely on costly clustering of high-dimensional correspondence features, motivating a different way to organize the search for multiple poses.

PointMC builds a correspondence compatibility graph and searches it for maximal cliques: groups of correspondences that are mutually compatible and cannot be expanded while preserving that property. It uses these groups to estimate candidate transformations, then clusters the transformations into groups associated with different instances. This places the clustering step at the level of estimated transformations.

A correspondence embedding module uses local spatial consistency to remove outliers. Its discriminative features also help avoid missing poses when instances overlap, directly addressing the scenario that challenges existing approaches. Experiments on synthetic and real-world datasets report substantial performance improvements. The results support combining local correspondence filtering with clique-based transformation estimation for accurate and efficient recovery of multiple instance poses.
icml-2024-pointmc-multi-instance-point-c.tldr: PointMC uses mutually compatible correspondence groups to estimate and cluster multiple poses, including when point-cloud instances overlap.

paragraphs: Decision-makers often care about both immediate benefits and the eventual effects of an intervention. This paper formalizes policy learning that balances short-term and long-term rewards while allowing some long-term outcomes to be missing. The goal is to learn a decision policy that accounts for both horizons instead of letting attention to one obscure the other.

The authors establish that both rewards are identifiable under assumptions they describe as mild. They derive semiparametric efficiency bounds and show consistency and asymptotic normality for their estimators. These results describe the estimators’ statistical behavior and the achievable precision of reward estimation. They also show that short-term outcomes can improve long-term reward estimation when the outcomes are associated.

Using these estimators, the paper develops a policy-learning approach and derives convergence rates for its regret and estimation errors. Extensive experiments support the method’s effectiveness. The contribution therefore connects reward identification, statistically grounded estimation, and policy choice in a single framework that accommodates incomplete observations of long-term outcomes.
icml-2024-policy-learning-for-balancing-.tldr: The paper develops statistically grounded policy learning that balances short-term and long-term rewards despite some missing long-term outcomes.

paragraphs: A frequency profile records what fraction of a domain’s items appear zero times, once, twice, and so on in a multiset. This paper studies how to estimate that profile from a private, updatable sketch in a distributed setting with limited storage. The target is the distribution of occurrence counts across the domain.

The method starts with a histogram made differentially private using discrete Laplace noise. It adapts an existing approach to reverse the noise’s effect for profile estimation. The authors accelerate the computation from polynomial time to O(d + n log n), where d is the domain size and n is the number of items in the multiset.

They analyze error under three norms, each yielding an O(1/sqrt(d)) dependence on domain size. An information-theoretic lower bound shows this dependence is asymptotically optimal among private, updatable sketches with a high-probability error guarantee. The result establishes optimality for that particular dependence and class of guarantees while also providing a faster reconstruction procedure.
icml-2024-profile-reconstruction-from-pr.tldr: The paper speeds up private frequency-profile reconstruction and proves optimal domain-size dependence for its error guarantees.

paragraphs: Fluid-dynamics models need to remain useful when environmental conditions differ from those seen during training. The paper introduces Prometheus, a large-scale dataset of simulated tunnel and pool fires under varied conditions. A benchmark of 12 baselines shows that out-of-distribution generalization remains unsatisfactory, establishing a concrete testbed for this challenge.

The proposed Disentangled Graph ODE model separates information from historical trajectories into node and environment representations. A temporal graph neural network extracts node information, while a frequency network extracts environmental information. Adversarial learning minimizes mutual information between invariant node representations and discretized environmental features, aiming to reduce the dependence that could make node representations vulnerable to distribution shifts.

The representations feed a coupled graph ordinary differential equation framework that models continuous evolution using neighboring nodes and changing environmental context. Perturbing environment features further improves stability and robustness. Experiments show the method’s effectiveness relative to state-of-the-art approaches, supporting the combination of representation separation and continuous interaction modeling on the evaluated fluid-dynamics tasks.
icml-2024-prometheus-out-of-distribution.tldr: Prometheus benchmarks fluid-dynamics generalization, while DGODE separates node and environment information to improve performance under changing conditions.

paragraphs: Protein surfaces contain information about how proteins interact, but surface-based learning has received less attention than learning from amino acid sequences or three-dimensional structures. Surface-VQMAE explores unsupervised pretraining using molecular surfaces alone. Its design addresses the fact that surface point clouds are sparse and have no inherent sequence ordering.

The method divides a surface into patches and arranges them using a Morton curve. A Transformer architecture called SurfFormer then integrates surface geometry and models relationships between patches. The framework adds vector quantization to a masked autoencoder, creating a codebook of surface patterns and a discrete representation of latent variables intended to capture more compact semantic information.

The resulting pipeline turns unordered surface measurements into structured, reusable representations of interaction-related patterns. Evaluations include binding-site scoring, binding-affinity prediction, and mutation-effect estimation, with extensive experiments demonstrating effectiveness across these tasks. The findings support molecular surfaces as a useful basis for pretraining and show how patch organization, geometric modeling, and a discrete pattern codebook can work together.
icml-2024-surface-vqmae-vector-quantized.tldr: Surface-VQMAE learns discrete molecular-surface patterns through unsupervised pretraining for protein interaction and mutation-related prediction tasks.

paragraphs: Partial differential equations are often represented on large meshes with complex geometry. Applying Transformers directly to their many individual points makes physical relationships difficult to capture efficiently. Transolver instead learns representations of the physical states underlying those points, using them to organize the computation.

Its Physics-Attention mechanism adaptively divides the discretized domain into learnable slices with flexible shapes. Points with similar physical states are assigned to the same slice, and each slice is encoded into a physics-aware token. Attention operates on these tokens to capture relationships across the domain. This construction supports modeling across general geometries and can be computed with linear complexity.

The paper reports consistent state-of-the-art performance and a 22% relative gain across six standard benchmarks. It also reports strong results in large-scale industrial simulations involving car and airfoil designs. These findings support grouping mesh points by learned physical state as a useful way to combine computational efficiency with the ability to represent intricate physical correlations on complex domains.
icml-2024-transolver-a-fast-transformer-.tldr: Transolver groups mesh points into learned physical-state slices to solve PDEs efficiently across complex geometries.

paragraphs: Modern Hopfield models retrieve stored patterns through energy minimization. This paper introduces U-Hop, a two-stage method that changes the representation of memories before performing retrieval. Its goal is to increase memory capacity and reduce confusion caused by competing or metastable states in the energy landscape.

A learnable feature map transforms the energy function into a kernel space, where its induced norm supplies a new similarity measure. The stored memories themselves provide the learning data. In the first stage, a separation loss pushes stored patterns apart in that space, spreading the associated energy minima more uniformly. The second stage performs standard Hopfield energy minimization to retrieve a memory.

The formulation aligns local energy minima with retrieval fixed points in the kernel space and substantially reduces possible metastable states. On real-world datasets, the authors report substantial gains over existing modern Hopfield models and state-of-the-art similarity measures in associative retrieval and deep-learning tasks. The results support learning a memory-specific similarity representation before running the retrieval dynamics.
icml-2024-uniform-memory-retrieval-with-.tldr: U-Hop learns to separate stored memories in kernel space before retrieval, increasing capacity and reducing memory confusion.

paragraphs: Positive-unlabeled learning uses known positive examples alongside examples whose labels are unknown. On graphs, connections between nodes add information but can also undermine learning. This paper identifies edge heterophily, where connected nodes have different labels, as a central difficulty for this setting.

The analysis finds that heterophily violates the irreducibility assumption used in estimating the class prior, a quantity needed for building positive-unlabeled learning algorithms. It also degrades inference of hidden labels on unlabeled nodes during classifier training. The issue therefore affects both estimating the class balance and using graph relationships to learn predictions.

The proposed GPL method incorporates an intermediate heterophily-reduction step into learning from positive and unlabeled nodes. It expresses the process as bilevel optimization: an inner loop reduces heterophily, while an outer loop trains the classifier. Experiments across varied datasets show significant gains over baseline methods. These findings support explicitly addressing graph structure when adapting positive-unlabeled learning, because problematic connections can interfere with multiple parts of the learning pipeline.
icml-2024-unraveling-the-impact-of-heter.tldr: GPL improves graph positive-unlabeled learning by reducing heterophily within a bilevel classifier-training procedure.

paragraphs: Zero-shot object navigation asks an agent to find objects from novel categories in unfamiliar environments without explicit prior training for those categories. VoroNav addresses this task by translating an evolving spatial map into information a large language model can use to choose navigation waypoints.

The framework constructs a semantic map in real time and derives a Reduced Voronoi Graph to identify exploration paths and planning nodes. It combines topological and semantic information into text descriptions of paths and visual observations. Path and farsight descriptions jointly represent the surrounding context, allowing the language model to apply commonsense reasoning when deciding where the agent should go next.

On HM3D, the paper reports absolute improvements of 2.8% in success and 3.7% in SPL; on HSSD, the corresponding improvements are 2.6% and 3.8%. Additional measures of obstacle avoidance and perceptual efficiency also support the method’s benefits. The results indicate that structured environmental descriptions can help translate language-model reasoning into more successful and efficient exploration.
icml-2024-voronav-voronoi-based-zero-sho.tldr: VoroNav turns semantic maps into path descriptions that help a language model choose effective waypoints for zero-shot object navigation.
